Below is a complete empirical research plan tailored to your question and data.

1. Identification Strategy

- Method: Panel difference-in-differences with instrumental variables (2SLS), implemented as a high-dimensional FE IV panel.
- Rationale:
  - Utilities set different nonlinear (tiered) schedules over time, and customers cannot choose their provider. The unusual service boundary within the same cities creates quasi-experimental, plausibly exogenous price-schedule variation across neighboring households with similar fundamentals.
  - The key challenge is endogeneity of realized marginal price under nonlinear pricing (marginal price is mechanically higher when demand is higher). We address this with simulated instruments that shift the relevant price measure using only exogenous schedule parameters (by utility-month) and exogenous predictors of consumption known at the start of the billing period, not the realized billing shock.
  - DID comes from comparing SCE vs SDG&E within the same city and month; IV comes from utility-by-month schedule changes applied to pre-period predicted consumption to form simulated marginal/average/expected marginal price. This allows us to estimate which price concept consumers actually respond to.


2. Treatment and Control

- Treatment variable(s): Continuous price measure(s) faced by household i in billing period t under its assigned utility u:
  - Marginal price (MP_it): marginal price at realized consumption under the assigned utility’s nonlinear schedule.
  - Average price (AP_it): bill_it / kWh_it.
  - Expected marginal price (EMP_it): the marginal price a consumer would expect at the start of the billing cycle given their predictable consumption; we will operationalize EMP_it as the marginal price evaluated at predicted consumption q̂_it, with alternative constructions using the expected value over a forecast distribution.
- Instrument(s) for each endogenous price measure:
  - Simulated marginal price (SMP_it): MP(schedule_{u,t}, q̂_it), where schedule_{u,t} is the full set of tier thresholds and prices for utility u in month t, and q̂_it is predicted kWh based only on pre-period household fixed effect and exogenous weather in period t.
  - Simulated average price (SAP_it): AP(schedule_{u,t}, q̂_it).
  - Simulated expected marginal price (SEMP_it): same as SMP_it (baseline definition) or an integrated expectation over the pre-period consumption distribution (robustness).
- Control group/counterfactual: Households in the other utility’s service area but in the same city-month serve as the counterfactual for local shocks. We implement this via city-by-calendar-month fixed effects that net out city-specific weather, shocks, and seasonality.
- Treatment timing: Continuous over 1999–2007 as schedules change on different dates by utility (e.g., 2000 SDG&E spikes; 2001 shift to 5 tiers). The main panel IV does not require specific event dates, but we will also implement event-study robustness around discrete tariff changes.
- No RDD: Although there is a geographic boundary, a static spatial RDD cannot isolate marginal vs average price responses because both differ across utilities. Time variation and instruments are necessary to separate price concepts.


3. Key Identifying Assumptions

- A1. Exogeneity of utility assignment: Customers cannot select their provider; assignment is by address, and we restrict to “stayers” at the same premise. Plausible given the institutional rules.
- A2. As-good-as-random tariff shocks within city over time: Conditional on city-by-month fixed effects and household fixed effects, changes in the assigned utility’s schedule are orthogonal to idiosyncratic demand shocks at the household level. Plausible: CPUC approval and utility cost shocks are system-wide and not targeted at neighborhoods along the internal boundary.
- A3. Instrument validity (exclusion): Simulated prices depend only on exogenous schedule parameters (utility-month) and q̂_it based on pre-period household fixed effects and contemporaneous weather; they affect consumption only through the price concept and not through other channels. Plausible if we:
  - Estimate q̂_it using only pre-period data and exogenous weather.
  - Control finely for local shocks via city-by-month FE and rich weather controls aligned to the billing window.
- A4. No differential non-price programs by utility that vary within the same city-month and correlate with schedule changes: If SDG&E and SCE differentially deploy DSM/rebate programs at the same time in the same split cities, this could violate exclusion. We will check for and control for available DSM program intensity proxies; absent such data, city-by-utility-by-year FE can help absorb slow-moving differences.
- A5. No strategic sorting or spillovers at the boundary during the sample: With stayers only, migration or switching is limited; spillovers (e.g., peer effects across the boundary) are unlikely to coincide precisely with utility-month schedule changes. Plausible; we will test for it via pretrends and spatial robustness (e.g., results stable when trimming to blocks closest to the boundary).


4. Threats to Identification and Remedies

- T1. Price endogeneity from nonlinear budget sets (tier selection): Higher idiosyncratic demand drives both higher consumption and higher realized MP. Remedy: Use simulated instruments (SMP, SAP, SEMP) based on schedule parameters and pre-period predicted consumption that excludes the period-specific demand shock. Also include household FE and city-by-month FE to net out time-invariant heterogeneity and local shocks.
- T2. Differential DSM/programs or billing-rule differences across utilities: If program rollouts or non-price changes correlate with price changes within the same city-month, exclusion could fail. Remedies:
  - Include utility-by-year FE and city-by-utility linear trends to absorb slow-moving utility differences.
  - Where available, control for zip/block-group DSM participation or program eligibility proxies.
  - Event-study pretrends around major tariff changes to test for anticipatory or coincident non-price shocks.
- T3. Weather and billing-cycle misalignment: Different meter-read dates can misalign weather exposure across utilities. Remedies:
  - Convert to daily kWh (kWh/day) and align weather to each customer’s billing window using degree-days aggregated over start–end dates. Include flexible weather controls (CDD, HDD, quadratic terms, interactions with climate zone).
  - Control for billing days and meter-read-cycle fixed effects.


5. R Code Outline

Note: This is an executable template. You will need to adapt file paths and tariff format. We assume three CSVs: billing.csv (household bills), tariffs.csv (utility-month tier thresholds and prices), weather.csv (zip9-by-day temps). We calendarize to billing windows and create simulated instruments.

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(lubridate)
library(fixest)
library(stringr)
library(dplyr)

#-----------------------------
# 1) Load data
#-----------------------------
bill <- fread("billing.csv")  # columns: acct_id, premise_id, utility, city, zip9, bill_start, bill_end, kwh, bill_amount, tariff, climate_zone
tar  <- fread("tariffs.csv")  # columns: utility, ym (YYYY-MM), tier, price_cents_kwh, threshold_kwh_per_day (up to tier K; last tier threshold = Inf or NA)
wday <- fread("weather_daily.csv") # columns: zip9, date, tmax_c, tmin_c

# Keep main analytic sample (six cities, standard residential tariff, stayers)
cities_keep <- c("Laguna Beach","Laguna Niguel","Aliso Viejo","Laguna Hills","Mission Viejo","Coto de Caza")
bill <- bill[city %in% cities_keep & tariff=="standard_residential"]

# Restrict to stayers at same premise over full period observed for that premise
stay <- bill[ , .(premises_n = uniqueN(premise_id)), by=.(acct_id)]
# Actually we want each (acct_id) tied to same premise across their observed months
# Keep only acct_id with one premise_id:
one_prem <- bill[ , .(premises_n = uniqueN(premise_id)), by=acct_id][premises_n==1, acct_id]
bill <- bill[acct_id %in% one_prem]

# Dates and billing days
bill[ , `:=`(
  start = as.Date(bill_start),
  end   = as.Date(bill_end),
  days  = as.integer(end - start) + 1L,
  ym    = format(end, "%Y-%m")
)]
bill <- bill[days>0 & kwh>0]  # drop obvious errors
bill[ , kwh_per_day := kwh / days]
bill[ , avg_price_cents := (bill_amount / kwh) * 100]  # average price in cents/kWh

#-----------------------------
# 2) Weather alignment to billing window
#-----------------------------
# Compute HDD/CDD relative to base 65F (18C)
degday_fun <- function(tmin_c, tmax_c, base_c=18) {
  tavg_c <- (tmin_c + tmax_c)/2
  hdd <- pmax(0, base_c - tavg_c)
  cdd <- pmax(0, tavg_c - base_c)
  list(hdd=hdd, cdd=cdd)
}
dd <- wday[ , {
  ddv <- degday_fun(tmin_c, tmax_c)
  .(hdd=ddv$hdd, cdd=ddv$cdd)
}, by=.(zip9, date)]

# Expand bills to daily to sum degree-days over exact billing windows
# (memory-aware rolling join)
bill_daily <- bill[ , .(acct_id, premise_id, utility, city, zip9, start, end, days, ym)][, .(date=seq(start, end, by="day")), by=.(acct_id, premise_id, utility, city, zip9, start, end, days, ym)]
setkey(bill_daily, zip9, date)
setkey(dd, zip9, date)
bill_daily <- dd[bill_daily, nomatch=0]
# Aggregate degree-days back to bill period
w_agg <- bill_daily[ , .(
  hdd = sum(hdd, na.rm=TRUE),
  cdd = sum(cdd, na.rm=TRUE)
), by=.(acct_id, premise_id, utility, city, zip9, start, end, days, ym)]
bill <- merge(bill, w_agg, by=c("acct_id","premise_id","utility","city","zip9","start","end","days","ym"))

#-----------------------------
# 3) Build tariff schedule objects per utility-month
#-----------------------------
# Ensure thresholds are in kWh per day; convert to total kWh over the customer's days later
# We will keep a list of schedules by (utility, ym)
setorder(tar, utility, ym, tier)
# Check last tier threshold; if NA, set to Inf
tar[is.na(threshold_kwh_per_day), threshold_kwh_per_day := Inf]

# Function to compute bill and marginal price given q (kWh) and schedule (thresholds per day, prices)
compute_bill_mp <- function(q, days, thresh_per_day, prices_cents) {
  # thresholds in kWh for the whole bill:
  th <- pmin(thresh_per_day, Inf) * days
  # cumulative thresholds
  th_cum <- th
  # Convert to finite vector with last = Inf
  th_cum[length(th_cum)] <- Inf
  # Quantities in each tier
  q_tier <- numeric(length(prices_cents))
  remain <- q
  prev <- 0
  for (k in seq_along(prices_cents)) {
    cap <- th_cum[k]
    take <- pmax(0, pmin(remain, cap - prev))
    q_tier[k] <- take
    remain <- remain - take
    prev <- cap
    if (remain <= 0) break
  }
  bill_cents <- sum(q_tier * prices_cents)
  # marginal price = price of the tier where last kWh lies
  cumq <- cumsum(q_tier)
  k_star <- which(cumq >= q)[1]
  mp_cents <- prices_cents[k_star]
  list(bill_cents=bill_cents, mp_cents=mp_cents)
}

# Prepare a fast lookup table of schedules by utility-month
tar_list <- split(tar, by=c("utility","ym"), keep.by=FALSE)

# Helper to get schedule vectors
get_sched <- function(utility, ym) {
  key <- paste0(utility,"_",ym)
  tt <- tar_list[[key]]
  if (is.null(tt)) return(NULL)
  list(thresh=tt$threshold_kwh_per_day, prices=tt$price_cents_kwh)
}

#-----------------------------
# 4) Construct realized price measures and simulated instruments
#-----------------------------
# Realized MP/AP from observed bill and kWh: AP already built. For MP, we need q and schedule.
bill[ , `:=`(mp_cents=NA_real_)]

for (i in seq_len(nrow(bill))) {
  sc <- get_sched(bill$utility[i], bill$ym[i])
  if (is.null(sc)) next
  res <- compute_bill_mp(q=bill$kwh[i], days=bill$days[i], thresh_per_day=sc$thresh, prices_cents=sc$prices)
  bill$mp_cents[i] <- res$mp_cents
  # Sanity: could also recompute bill and compare to bill_amount; optional
}

# Build pre-period (1999–2000) model to predict consumption as function of HH FE and weather
bill[ , year := year(end)]
pre <- bill[year %in% c(1999,2000)]
# Estimate: kWh/day on HH FE + CDD + HDD (and their squares)
pre_mod <- feols(kwh_per_day ~ cdd + hdd + I(cdd^2) + I(hdd^2) | acct_id, data=pre)
# Predict qhat for all periods using estimated coefficients plus HH FE from pre-period
bill[ , kwhpd_hat := predict(pre_mod, newdata=bill)]
# Clip at small positive values
bill[ kwhpd_hat < 0.1, kwhpd_hat := 0.1]
bill[ , qhat := kwhpd_hat * days]

# Simulated instruments: apply current schedule to qhat
bill[ , `:=`(smp_cents=NA_real_, sap_cents=NA_real_, semp_cents=NA_real_)]

for (i in seq_len(nrow(bill))) {
  sc <- get_sched(bill$utility[i], bill$ym[i])
  if (is.null(sc)) next
  res <- compute_bill_mp(q=bill$qhat[i], days=bill$days[i], thresh_per_day=sc$thresh, prices_cents=sc$prices)
  bill$smp_cents[i] <- res$mp_cents
  bill$sap_cents[i] <- (res$bill_cents / bill$qhat[i])  # cents/kWh at predicted q
  bill$semp_cents[i] <- res$mp_cents  # baseline defn: EMP at predicted q
}

# Controls and fixed effects identifiers
bill[ , `:=`(
  ln_kwh = log(kwh),
  util_month = paste0(utility,"_",ym),
  city_month = paste0(city,"_",ym)
)]

#-----------------------------
# 5) Main 2SLS specifications
#-----------------------------
# Cluster two-way: household and utility-month
# Spec A: Response to marginal price
mod_mp <- feols(
  ln_kwh ~ cdd + hdd + I(cdd^2) + I(hdd^2) + days | acct_id + city_month ~  mp_cents | smp_cents,
  data = bill,
  cluster = ~ acct_id + util_month
)

# Spec B: Response to average price
mod_ap <- feols(
  ln_kwh ~ cdd + hdd + I(cdd^2) + I(hdd^2) + days | acct_id + city_month ~  avg_price_cents | sap_cents,
  data = bill,
  cluster = ~ acct_id + util_month
)

# Spec C: Response to expected marginal price (baseline defn at predicted q)
mod_emp <- feols(
  ln_kwh ~ cdd + hdd + I(cdd^2) + I(hdd^2) + days | acct_id + city_month ~  mp_cents | semp_cents,
  data = bill,
  cluster = ~ acct_id + util_month
)

# Spec D: Horse race including all three (requires multiple endogenous regressors and instruments)
# Build EMP as a separate endogenous regressor if different from MP (here same baseline defn);
# For illustration, use three measures: realized MP, realized AP, and EMP_alt (see robustness below).
# Suppose we created emp_alt_cents and semp_alt_cents; then:
# mod_horse <- feols(
#   ln_kwh ~ cdd + hdd + I(cdd^2) + I(hdd^2) + days | acct_id + city_month ~ 
#            cbind(mp_cents, avg_price_cents, emp_alt_cents) | 
#            cbind(smp_cents, sap_cents, semp_alt_cents),
#   data = bill, cluster = ~ acct_id + util_month
# )

summary(mod_mp)
summary(mod_ap)
summary(mod_emp)

#-----------------------------
# 6) Robustness checks
#-----------------------------

# R1: Alternative instrument for EMP using forecast distribution (expected MP)
# Construct emp_alt as the expected marginal price integrating over a household-specific forecast distribution
# Use past 3 same-months (leave-current-out) to form a discrete distribution of qtilde; apply current schedule; take average MP
bill[ , mth := month(end)]
hist_q <- bill[ , .(qhist=list(kwh[mth==unique(mth) & year<year(end)][1:3])), by=.(acct_id, mth, ym, utility)]
# Merge and compute expected MP instrument
bill <- merge(bill, hist_q, by=c("acct_id","mth","ym","utility"), all.x=TRUE)
bill[ , `:=`(emp_alt_cents=NA_real_, semp_alt_cents=NA_real_)]
for (i in seq_len(nrow(bill))) {
  sc <- get_sched(bill$utility[i], bill$ym[i])
  if (is.null(sc)) next
  qv <- bill$qhist[[i]]
  if (length(qv)==0) next
  mps <- vapply(qv, function(qi) compute_bill_mp(q=qi, days=bill$days[i], thresh_per_day=sc$thresh, prices_cents=sc$prices)$mp_cents, numeric(1))
  bill$emp_alt_cents[i] <- NA_real_  # realized expected MP not used directly
  bill$semp_alt_cents[i] <- mean(mps) # instrument based on historical q's
}

mod_emp_alt <- feols(
  ln_kwh ~ cdd + hdd + I(cdd^2) + I(hdd^2) + days | acct_id + city_month ~ mp_cents | semp_alt_cents,
  data=bill, cluster=~acct_id + util_month
)
summary(mod_emp_alt)

# R2: Event-study around major SDG&E 2000 spike and 2001 five-tier introduction (outline)
# Build an indicator for treated utility-periods and event time, include city FE and calendar-month FE
# (Requires a tariff_changes.csv with utility, event_date; omitted here due to data dependency)
```

Notes:
- The simulated instruments vary at utility-month and across households through q̂_it (from pre-period HH FE and contemporaneous weather). This provides within-city-month quasi-experimental variation in price measures while holding city-month shocks constant.
- If DSM data are available at zip/block-group, add them as controls. You can also add utility-by-year FE and city-by-utility linear trends.


6. Expected Results

- Direction:
  - If consumers fully optimize on the true marginal price, the elasticity to MP should be negative and meaningful in magnitude.
  - With complex, nonlinear bills, many households likely anchor on average or expected (start-of-period) marginal price rather than the contemporaneous realized marginal price.
- Magnitude:
  - Short-run residential electricity elasticities are commonly around -0.1 to -0.3. My prior:
    - Elasticity to average price: around -0.15 to -0.20.
    - Elasticity to expected marginal price: similar to or slightly smaller than AP (e.g., -0.10 to -0.15), depending on forecast error.
    - Elasticity to realized contemporaneous marginal price (computed at end-of-cycle consumption): near zero to modest (-0.05), reflecting endogeneity and limited salience.
- Implications:
  - If AP or EMP explains consumption better than MP, steep tiered pricing is a blunt tool for marginal incentives; it reduces consumption primarily through higher average bills (income/scale effects), potentially generating larger deadweight loss for a given marginal incentive. Welfare simulations would use the estimated elasticities with each pricing concept to compute counterfactual consumption and surplus under alternative tariff designs.


7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment

- C1: Exogenous assignment to utility (address-based, no choice) and stayers-only sample. Rating: 1
- C2: Parallel trends/local common shocks captured by city-by-month FE; no utility-specific time-varying shocks within city-month aside from tariffs. Rating: 1 (to be validated with pretrends)
- C3: Instrument relevance (large, repeated utility-by-month schedule shifts interacted with exogenous q̂_it). Rating: 1
- C4: Exclusion restriction for simulated instruments (constructed from pre-period HH FE and weather; controls absorb local shocks). Rating: 1 (subject to DSM checks)
- C5: No spillovers or contemporaneous differential non-price programs within the same city-month correlated with price changes. Rating: 0 (plausible but needs verification and controls)

This plan yields causal estimates of the demand response to different price concepts under nonlinear pricing, leveraging the unique boundary setting and repeated independent tariff shocks.
